stimuli.title: Carbon in the soil
stimuli.body:
For much of the twentieth century, soil scientists described the storage of carbon in soil as a story about plants. Leaves and roots fall to the ground, the reasoning went, and the portion that resists decay slowly turns into humus, a dark, complex material that can remain in the soil for centuries. On this view, the way to increase the carbon stored in farmland was to return as much plant residue to the soil as possible, particularly tough, woody residue that decomposes slowly.

Recent work has complicated that picture. Using techniques that can trace individual carbon atoms through the soil, researchers have found that much of the carbon that persists for long periods is not woody plant material at all, but the remains of microbes. Easily digested plant matter, such as fresh leaves, is quickly consumed by bacteria and fungi, and although much of it is released as carbon dioxide, a fraction is built into microbial bodies. When these microbes die, their cell fragments bind tightly to fine mineral particles, which shield them from further decay. Paradoxically, then, the material that decomposes fastest may contribute most to long-term storage.

This finding does not overturn the older view entirely. Tough plant residue still matters, particularly in cold, waterlogged soils where microbes are sluggish. But it suggests that farm management practices designed around the old model, such as favouring slow-decomposing residue, may deserve a second look.

stimuli.title: The card-on-file trial
stimuli.body:
Software companies have long debated whether to ask for payment details at the start of a free trial. The conventional case against doing so is easy to state: every extra field on a sign-up form loses some prospective customers, and a customer who never starts a trial can never become a paying one. Companies that adopted this reasoning generally allowed anyone to try their product with only an email address.

A study of eleven subscription software firms suggests the conventional case is less strong than it seems. When firms began requiring a card at sign-up, the number of trials started fell by roughly half. But the proportion of trial users who went on to pay rose from about one in ten to about one in six, so that the number of paying customers fell by much less than the number of trials. Moreover, customers who had entered a card were less likely to cancel in their first year, perhaps because they had already made a small commitment to the product.

The authors are careful to note a limit. The firms in the study sold tools that users employ daily, such as scheduling and invoicing software, where a few days of use is enough to show the value of the product. For products whose benefits emerge slowly, such as language courses, a card requirement might screen out the very customers who would have been won over by a longer, lower-pressure trial. The lesson, they conclude, is not that card-required trials are better, but that the number of sign-ups is a poor measure of a trial's success.

stimuli.title: Counting readers
stimuli.body:
Historians who want to know how many ordinary people could read in early modern Europe face an awkward problem: ordinary people left few records of their reading. Since the nineteenth century, many scholars have therefore relied on a proxy. Marriage registers in many countries required bride and groom to sign their names, or else to make a mark, and the share who signed is commonly treated as a measure of literacy.

The method has real virtues. The registers are abundant, they cover rich and poor, and they allow comparison across regions and decades. Yet a growing number of historians argue that signature rates measure something narrower than literacy. In many communities, children were taught to read first, often at home or in church, and taught to write only later, if at all, because writing required paper, pens and fee-paying instruction. A woman who could read a prayer book fluently but had never held a pen would appear in the register as illiterate. If this was common, signature counts would systematically understate reading ability, particularly among women and the poor.

The point should not be pressed too far. Signature rates remain a reliable guide to trends over time, since the gap between reading and writing probably changed slowly. What they cannot do, these historians conclude, is establish how many people could read at any given moment. Treating a signature count as a literacy rate, in short, mistakes a lower bound for a measurement.

stimuli.title: Film music and its critics
stimuli.body:
Critics of film music have often charged it with a lack of originality. The great scores of Hollywood's golden age, they note, borrowed freely from the harmonic language of late nineteenth-century opera, and composers such as Max Steiner openly acknowledged their debt to Wagner. If the idiom was inherited, the argument runs, the achievement of the film composer must be one of adaptation rather than invention.

This charge is accurate as far as it goes, but it mistakes the source of the film composer's difficulty. The opera composer controlled the pace of the drama; the film composer does not. A film arrives with its timing fixed, and the music must fit around spoken dialogue, sudden cuts and scenes whose length was decided by an editor, often after the composer has begun work. A theme that would unfold across several minutes on the stage must be compressed into forty seconds, or broken into fragments that can be rearranged when a scene is trimmed. These constraints produced techniques with no real precedent in the opera house: music that recedes beneath speech without disappearing, and motifs designed to be recognisable after only three or four notes.

None of this makes every film score a masterpiece, and the genre has produced its share of formulaic work. But to judge film music by the standards of originality of the concert hall is rather like criticising a sonnet for failing to be a novel. The more fruitful question is how well a composer has solved the problems that the medium sets.

stimuli.title: Wolves and willows
stimuli.body:
When wolves were returned to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, ecologists predicted a cascade of effects. Wolves would reduce the number of elk, the reasoning went, and the browsing elk, relieved of that pressure, would spare the young willows and aspens along the streams. Healthier willows would in turn shelter beavers and songbirds and stabilise stream banks. Within a decade, popular accounts were describing the park as a textbook case of an ecosystem restored by the return of a single predator. The story proved irresistible partly because it was so easy to tell: a single cause, a clear chain of consequences and a satisfying moral about the importance of top predators.

Subsequent fieldwork has been less tidy. Elk numbers did decline, but the decline began before the wolves arrived at full strength, and it coincided with a run of dry years, with hunting of elk outside the park, and with a recovery in the numbers of grizzly bears, which also prey on elk calves. Moreover, the recovery of willows has been uneven. Along some streams, young willows now stand taller than a browsing elk can reach; along others, they remain cropped to stubs. Researchers who stress the predator's influence note that the taller willows tend to grow where the terrain gives elk poor escape routes, suggesting that wolves change where elk feed rather than simply how many elk there are. Sceptics reply that this pattern would also arise if the willows were simply growing where the soil is wettest. Neither side disputes that the park looks different from how it did in the 1980s; the question is why.

The dispute is not merely academic. If wolves were the principal engine of recovery, then reintroducing predators elsewhere should yield comparable results, and conservation agencies have drawn on the Yellowstone story in making that case. If, on the other hand, the recovery reflects several forces acting together, the benefits of reintroduction will vary with the climate, the presence of other predators and the history of human hunting in each region. This is not an argument against reintroduction, which may be justified on other grounds. It is an argument for describing its ecological consequences with the caution that the evidence, so far, allows.

stimuli.title: Five stars for everyone
stimuli.body:
On most online marketplaces, the average rating of a seller is above four stars out of five, and the great majority of ratings are the maximum. Such compression is often described as grade inflation, and platform designers worry about it for an obvious reason: when nearly everyone is excellent, a rating no longer tells a buyer which seller to choose, even though sellers depend on ratings for visibility and the highest-ranked earn markedly more. The usual diagnosis is that reviewers are generous by temperament, or lazy, and the usual remedy is to ask for more detailed ratings in the hope that detail will force discrimination.

An alternative diagnosis points to the structure of the exchange rather than the psychology of the reviewer. On many platforms, buyers and sellers review each other, and a seller who receives a poor rating can respond in kind. Because the buyer anticipates this, a rational buyer with a modest complaint may prefer to say nothing, or to give five stars. Under this account, inflated ratings are not a sign of generosity but a sign of caution, and asking for more detailed ratings will do little, because the fear of retaliation applies to every field on the form.

Evidence for the second diagnosis comes from a platform that changed its rules so that neither party could see the other's review until both had been submitted. Average ratings given by buyers fell noticeably, and the share of buyers who left written criticism roughly doubled. The platform covered services ranging from home repairs to tutoring, and the change was introduced across all categories on the same day. Notably, the change had little effect on sellers' reviews of buyers, which were already candid, presumably because buyers have little to fear from a seller's rating.

None of this proves that temperament plays no role. Buyers do differ, and some will always be generous. But the experiment suggests that platform designers who treat ratings inflation as a problem of reviewer character may be treating the symptom rather than the cause. If so, the more promising reforms are those that remove the threat of retaliation, not those that merely ask reviewers to try harder.

stimuli.title: Seeds, water and prices
stimuli.body:
Accounts of the Green Revolution in India usually begin in the mid-1960s with a technological breakthrough: semi-dwarf wheat and rice varieties that responded to fertiliser with yields far above those of traditional seed. In the standard narrative, the seeds did the work. Farmers adopted them, harvests rose, and the food shortages that had forced India to rely on grain imports were left behind within a decade. Textbooks still tell it this way, in part because it offers a clean story with a clear hero, the plant breeder.

This narrative is not false, but historians of agriculture have long suspected that it assigns too much to the seed itself. The new varieties were demanding. They yielded well only with reliable water and purchased fertiliser, and they were of little use to a farmer without either. Fertiliser, too, had to be bought, often on credit, which favoured farmers with land to offer as security. Where canal or tube-well irrigation was already established, as in Punjab, adoption was rapid. Where it was not, as in much of eastern India, the same seeds produced disappointing results and were adopted slowly, if at all. In this sense the geography of the Green Revolution was largely a geography of irrigation that predated it.

Policy mattered as much as biology. The government guaranteed minimum prices for wheat and rice and bought grain on a large scale, which removed the price risk that would otherwise have discouraged farmers from investing in costly inputs. Subsidised fertiliser and cheap electricity for pumping completed the arrangement. Some economists have gone further and argued that the guaranteed prices, rather than the seed, were the decisive element. That claim is hard to test, since seeds and prices arrived together, and it is doubtful that it can be settled.

What can be said is that the seed was necessary but not sufficient. The revolution was a package, and its benefits fell to farmers who could assemble all of it. That helps to explain a feature that the standard narrative passes over: the gap between prosperous irrigated districts and the rest of the country widened in the decades that followed rather than narrowing.

stimuli.title: The shrinking brain
stimuli.body:
Over the past 30,000 years, the average volume of the human brain appears to have fallen by roughly a tenth, a loss about the size of a tennis ball. The observation, based on measurements of skulls from sites across several continents, has long troubled anthropologists, because it seems to run against the story of steadily increasing intelligence. Estimates differ from site to site, and individual brains vary widely, but the direction of the change is consistent. Three explanations dominate the literature.

The first holds that the shrinkage is a by-product of a smaller body. Larger animals generally need larger brains to manage larger bodies, and the people of the late Ice Age were, on average, more heavily built than their descendants. This account has the merit of simplicity, but it falls short on its own terms: the brain shrank by more than the standard scaling between brain and body size would predict.

A second explanation turns on social life. As human groups grew and became more interdependent, the argument goes, individuals no longer needed to hold so much knowledge in their own heads. Social groups, in this view, work as a shared memory. A farmer could rely on a blacksmith, and a traveller on a map. A brain that was cheap to run, given that it consumes about a fifth of the body's energy, would then have an advantage. The idea is attractive, but it is difficult to test, since it makes few predictions that differ from those of its rivals.

The third explanation is statistical. Skulls from the late Ice Age are rare, and those that survive may have come disproportionately from unusually large individuals, for example those buried with care. If so, the apparent decline may be partly a sampling effect. Proponents of this view concede that the decline would not vanish entirely if the sample were corrected, but suggest that it would shrink.

It would be a mistake to treat any of these accounts as settled, or to read the decline as evidence that modern humans think less well. Brain volume is a crude proxy: the organisation of the brain may matter more than its size, and nothing in the skull data speaks to that.

stimuli.title: Owning or franchising
stimuli.body:
Why do some retail and restaurant chains grow by franchising, while others insist on owning every outlet? For many years the textbook answer was financial. A young chain with a promising concept but little capital can expand faster by selling the right to operate outlets to local entrepreneurs, who put up their own money. Several well-known restaurant and hotel groups followed this route in their early years. On this account, franchising is a stage in a firm's life, to be outgrown: once the chain is large and profitable enough to borrow cheaply, it should buy back its franchises and run the outlets itself.

The prediction has not held up well. Many of the largest and most profitable chains in the world, with access to cheap capital, still franchise most of their outlets, and some have been selling company-owned outlets to franchisees rather than buying them. An alternative explanation, now widely accepted among economists, concentrates on incentives. A manager who is paid a salary to run an outlet that the head office cannot easily observe has little reason to work hard on a slow Tuesday afternoon. A franchisee who keeps the profit of the outlet has every reason. Franchising, in this view, is a way of purchasing effort that cannot be monitored directly, and the further an outlet lies from headquarters, the more valuable that purchase becomes.

The incentive account also explains a pattern that the financial one cannot: chains tend to keep company ownership of outlets near their headquarters, and franchise those that are remote. It is not, however, a complete theory. Franchising carries costs of its own. A franchisee may cut corners on quality, because the damage to the brand falls partly on other outlets, and the chain must spend heavily on inspection and on contracts to prevent this. Chains whose products depend on a consistent experience, such as hotels, therefore often hold on to ownership even in distant locations.

The two accounts are better seen as complementary than as rivals. Shortage of capital may explain why a chain starts franchising; the problem of monitoring may explain why it does not stop.

stimuli.title: The cleaning controversy
stimuli.body:
Few debates in the art world generate as much heat as the cleaning of old paintings. Over centuries, the varnish applied to protect an oil painting darkens and yellows, and dust and smoke settle on it, so that a canvas that left the studio bright may reach the modern viewer as a murky brown. When restorers remove the varnish, as they did with several celebrated works in the second half of the twentieth century, the results can be startling: skies turn blue again, and draperies that seemed black are revealed as deep green.

Critics of such cleanings have argued that they destroy something of value. Part of the pleasure of an old master, they say, lies in its mellow warmth, which later generations came to treat as part of the painter's achievement. Moreover, critics point out, painters of the period often finished their works with thin, translucent layers of glaze, and aggressive cleaning can remove these along with the varnish, leaving a picture harsher and flatter than its creator intended. There is, they add, a certain arrogance in the confidence of restorers who claim to know what the artist wished the picture to look like.

Restorers reply that the warmth admired by earlier generations was not a quality of the painting at all, but a symptom of its decay, and that the colour relationships on which the artist's design depended had been visibly distorted. Both sides, however, tend to treat the question as one with a single correct answer. This is mistaken. A painting is not a fixed object but one that has lived through changing conditions, and its history is part of what it is. Nor is it clear that the artist's intention, which is rarely documented, should be the only criterion.

A more productive approach is to shift the argument from what a picture should look like to what can be undone. Interventions that are reversible, and carefully recorded, leave later generations free to judge differently. Cleaning that destroys original material forecloses that freedom. On this view, the real failure of some celebrated restorations lies not in the brightness they restored, but in the irreversibility with which they achieved it.

stimuli.title: Lamps and pollinators
stimuli.body:
Streetlights and illuminated buildings have turned the night sky over much of the world into a permanent twilight, and ecologists have long suspected that this affects the insects that feed at night. Moths, in particular, are drawn to lamps, where they circle until they are exhausted or eaten. If moths are an important pollinator, as some botanists believe, then the spread of artificial light might be expected to harm the plants that depend on them.

A recent field study tested this prediction in meadows in southern England. The researchers placed lamps in half of the plots and left the rest dark, and then counted insect visits to flowers over three summers. Visits by moths in the lit plots fell by about three-fifths. Yet the number of seeds produced by the plants in those plots fell by only about one-eighth. The explanation appears to be that daytime pollinators, such as hoverflies and bees, visited the flowers in greater numbers when the moths were absent, making up much of the difference.

The authors do not conclude that artificial light is harmless. Most of the plants in the meadows could be pollinated by many species, and a loss of one group could easily be absorbed by others. A different result might be expected for plants with long, narrow flowers that only a few species of moth can reach, and the study was not designed to test those. For such plants, the authors suggest, the effect of light could be much greater than the figures from this study imply.

stimuli.title: Salary ranges in the open
stimuli.body:
Over the past decade, a number of jurisdictions have required employers to state a salary range in job advertisements. Advocates expected two benefits: job seekers would be better informed, and pay gaps between otherwise similar workers would narrow. Critics predicted that employers, no longer able to negotiate privately, would simply cut the top of the ranges they offer.

Early evidence supports both sides in part. In one study of ten regions, the pay gap between men and women in the same job narrowed by roughly a quarter within two years, which is consistent with the advocates' prediction. But average starting salaries for newly advertised jobs grew more slowly than in comparable regions without the requirement, which is consistent with the critics'. The slower growth was concentrated in firms that had previously paid above the market, suggesting that disclosure leads such firms to stop outbidding their rivals once the competition can see what they pay.

It would be premature to read these results as a verdict on the policy. A slower rise in starting salaries is not necessarily a loss for workers if it is offset by smaller differences between colleagues, and the studies cover too short a period to show whether longer-term wage growth is affected. What the evidence does show is that transparency changes behaviour on both sides of the market, and that its effects depend on how much employers were previously able to rely on secrecy. Whether the net result is favourable depends on which workers one has in mind: those hired at the top of a range lose what those hired at the bottom gain.

stimuli.title: Finishing the course
stimuli.body:
Patients prescribed antibiotics are routinely told to finish the entire course, even if they feel better after a few days. The advice has the force of common sense. Stopping early, the reasoning goes, leaves a few bacteria alive, and those survivors, being the hardiest, will multiply and give rise to a stronger infection. Doctors have repeated the instruction for decades, and it appears on the packaging of most antibiotics.

In recent years a number of researchers have questioned the advice. Their first objection concerns the evidence. The original recommendation arose largely from early work on tuberculosis, a disease with unusual features, and it was extended to other infections with little direct testing. When trials were eventually conducted for common illnesses such as pneumonia and urinary infections, shorter courses were found to work about as well as longer ones in most patients. Their second objection concerns the theory. The longer a patient takes an antibiotic, the longer the many harmless bacteria in the gut are exposed to it, and it is in that exposure, the critics argue, that resistance is most likely to develop. On this view the extra days of treatment do not eliminate hardy survivors but breed them.

Defenders of the traditional advice reply that the new trials have mostly involved mild infections in otherwise healthy adults, and that conclusions drawn from them should not be applied to patients with weakened immune systems or deep-seated infections such as those of the bone. They also note that stopping treatment is not the same as being prescribed a shorter course: the trials gave patients short courses of the correct length from the start, while a patient who simply stops when symptoms fade may stop before even a short course is complete.

The disagreement is therefore narrower than it first appears. Few researchers now claim that every infection should be treated for the shortest possible time; the question is whether the length of a course should be fixed by the illness, as the newer evidence suggests, rather than by habit. Until such trials are available for more kinds of infection, patients are best advised to follow the instructions of their own doctor rather than to adopt either slogan.

stimuli.title: Connected, but how?
stimuli.body:
For several decades, sociologists have lamented the decline of civic associations. Membership in trade unions, parent-teacher bodies, religious congregations and local clubs has fallen in many countries, and some scholars have drawn a gloomy conclusion: that people have become less connected to one another and that communities have lost the habits of cooperation on which democratic life depends. The argument is attractive because the numbers are real, and because the loss of a once-visible institution feels like an unmistakable sign of decline. In some countries the fall has been steep and sustained over several decades.

Yet the inference from falling membership to falling connection depends on an assumption that deserves scrutiny, namely that formal associations were the main way in which people used to form ties. A closer look at surveys suggests otherwise. In many places the share of people who report regular contact with neighbours, friends and colleagues has not fallen, and in some it has risen. What has changed is the form of the connection. Where an earlier generation joined a club that met on the first Monday of each month, a present-day resident is more likely to belong to a neighbourhood messaging group, or an informal circle of parents organised through a phone app, which has no officers, no dues and no minutes.

It would be too easy to conclude that nothing has been lost. Informal networks have virtues, among them flexibility and low cost, but they also have limits. They tend to form among people who are already similar in age, income and outlook, and they offer little protection to those who are not in them. A formal association with a written constitution had to admit new members who met its conditions; a group of friends need admit no one. If the older institutions were often dull and sometimes exclusive, they nevertheless gave strangers a reason to meet and a framework for resolving disputes.

The more useful question, then, is not whether people are more or less connected, but what kinds of connection are available to whom. On this question, the surveys are far less reassuring than their headline figures suggest.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the passage?
choices: To argue that tough plant residue plays no role in the long-term storage of soil carbon
To explain how techniques for tracing carbon atoms were developed
To compare the carbon content of cold, waterlogged soils with that of farmland
To show that bacteria and fungi are more valuable to agriculture than plants are
To present recent findings that qualify a long-held view of how soil stores carbon, and to suggest a consequence for farming
questions.explanation:
Map: P1 old view (plants and humus); P2 new evidence (microbial remains); P3 old view not fully overturned, farming practices deserve a second look.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. Paragraph 3 says the finding "does not overturn the older view entirely" and that tough residue "still matters".

(B) Wrong: Outside scope. The tracing techniques are mentioned only as the means by which the new finding was reached.

(C) Wrong: Too narrow. Cold, waterlogged soils appear only in one sentence of the last paragraph.

(D) Wrong: Overreach. The passage is about long-term carbon storage, not about the relative value of organisms to farming.

**(E) Correct.** It covers all three paragraphs: the old view, the new finding that qualifies it, and the farming implication.
questions.tip: A main-purpose answer must cover every paragraph; match the verb ("qualify") to how strongly the author pushes back.
questions.trap: Choosing the "no role at all" option because paragraph 2 sounds like a reversal; the author explicitly stops short of that in paragraph 3.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the remains of microbes can persist in soil for long periods because they
choices: are chemically tougher than woody plant residue
are quickly released as carbon dioxide
bind to fine mineral particles that shield them from further decay
are returned to the soil by farmers each season
are consumed by fungi only after several centuries
questions.explanation:
The answer is a direct paraphrase of one sentence in paragraph 2.

(A) Wrong: The passage never compares the chemical toughness of the two; the protection comes from minerals, not from toughness.

(B) Wrong: Reversed. Release as carbon dioxide is what happens to much of the easily digested plant matter, which is the opposite of persisting.

**(C) Correct.** Paragraph 2: "their cell fragments bind tightly to fine mineral particles, which shield them from further decay."

(D) Wrong: Farmers returning residue is part of the old model, not an explanation of microbial persistence.

(E) Wrong: Invented. Nothing in the passage describes fungi consuming microbial remains after centuries.
questions.tip: On detail questions, find the sentence containing the keyword ("persist") and match its paraphrase.
questions.trap: Picking "tougher than woody residue" because it sounds like a reason for persistence, even though the passage gives a different reason.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that in a warm, well-drained soil with highly active microbes, the long-lasting carbon is most likely to
choices: be absent, because microbes there break down all carbon
consist mainly of fresh leaves that remain intact for centuries
increase if farmers remove all plant residue after harvest
be unable to bind to mineral particles
derive largely from microbial remains rather than from tough plant residue
questions.explanation:
The inference is a small step from the contrast between sluggish microbes (tough residue matters) and active microbes (microbial remains matter).

(A) Wrong: Too extreme. Paragraph 2 says part of the carbon is built into microbial bodies and persists.

(B) Wrong: Contradicts paragraph 2: fresh leaves are consumed quickly.

(C) Wrong: Unsupported. The passage does not say that removing residue would increase storage; it only says old practices may deserve a second look.

(D) Wrong: No basis in the passage; binding to minerals is how microbial remains are protected generally.

**(E) Correct.** Paragraph 3 says tough residue matters "particularly in cold, waterlogged soils where microbes are sluggish". In soils with active microbes the contrast implies microbial remains carry more of the long-lasting carbon, consistent with paragraph 2.
questions.tip: When the passage says X matters "particularly" in condition A, a modest inference is that X matters less in the opposite condition.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme option ("absent", "all carbon") instead of the qualified one that the passage actually supports.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that software firms should require a card at sign-up for every product
explain why customers cancel subscriptions during their first year
report a study that challenges a common assumption about free trials while noting a limit on its conclusions
defend the conventional view that extra sign-up fields cost companies customers
compare how eleven firms design their sign-up forms
questions.explanation:
Map: P1 conventional case; P2 study challenges it; P3 limit and conclusion that sign-ups are a poor success measure.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The final sentence says the lesson "is not that card-required trials are better".

(B) Wrong: Too narrow. Cancellation is one supporting detail in paragraph 2.

**(C) Correct.** P1 states the assumption, P2 reports the study that challenges it, P3 gives the limit and a measured lesson.

(D) Wrong: Reversed. The passage says the conventional case is "less strong than it seems".

(E) Wrong: The study compares outcomes before and after a card requirement, not form design across firms.
questions.tip: In a "report, then qualify" passage, the correct purpose answer includes both the challenge and the caution.
questions.trap: Choosing the bold option that turns the study into a recommendation the authors explicitly decline to make.

questions.prompt: The author mentions language courses in order to
choices: identify a kind of product for which the study's findings might not hold
show that the study sample included products with slow-emerging benefits
provide evidence that card requirements raise first-year cancellations
argue that all free trials should be long and low-pressure
illustrate why sign-up forms should contain fewer fields
questions.explanation:
Find the general claim the example serves: the authors "note a limit" to their findings.

**(A) Correct.** Paragraph 3: for products whose benefits emerge slowly, such as language courses, a card requirement "might screen out" customers a longer trial would win.

(B) Wrong: Opposite. Paragraph 3 says the study firms sold tools used daily.

(C) Wrong: Paragraph 2 says card entry made cancellation less likely, and language courses are not offered as evidence of anything about cancellations.

(D) Wrong: Too strong. The point concerns slow-benefit products only, and the authors do not condemn card requirements generally.

(E) Wrong: This is the conventional case in paragraph 1, which the passage questions.
questions.tip: For an example question, identify the claim just before it ("a limit") and choose the answer that links the example to it.
questions.trap: Picking the answer that reverses the role of the example (as evidence from the study) rather than as a boundary on the study.

questions.prompt: Based on the authors' reasoning, requiring a card at sign-up would be most likely to reduce a firm's number of paying customers if the firm sold
choices: a course for a professional certification whose value becomes clear only after several weeks of lessons
a calendar tool that users open each morning and judge useful within days
an invoicing tool whose value is evident once the first invoice is sent
a team-messaging application that employees use constantly
a note-taking application that people try in their first session
questions.explanation:
Principle from paragraph 3: the card requirement is risky when benefits emerge slowly and safe when a few days of use show the value.

**(A) Correct.** This matches the limit in paragraph 3: slow-emerging benefits mean a lower-pressure, longer trial might win customers whom a card requirement screens out.

(B) Wrong: Matches the study's products (daily tools), where the higher conversion rate offset the loss of trials.

(C) Wrong: Value is visible quickly, so the study's result would be expected to hold.

(D) Wrong: Constant use shows value fast, again like the study's products.

(E) Wrong: Quick value again; no reason to expect the card requirement to cost paying customers.
questions.tip: For application questions, extract the condition under which the author's result fails, then find the scenario that meets it.
questions.trap: Overlooking that four choices describe products like those in the study, which is why they are wrong.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, signature counts may understate reading ability because
choices: marriage registers were kept only for the wealthiest families
bride and groom were forbidden from signing their names
many people were taught to read without being taught to write
children were taught to write before they were taught to read
many signatures in the registers were forged by officials
questions.explanation:
This is a paraphrase of the central claim of paragraph 2.

(A) Wrong: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says the registers "cover rich and poor".

(B) Wrong: Reversed. The registers required them to sign or make a mark.

**(C) Correct.** Paragraph 2: children were "taught to read first" and "to write only later, if at all", so readers who could not sign appear illiterate.

(D) Wrong: Reversed. The passage says reading came first.

(E) Wrong: Never mentioned; the passage gives no hint of forgery.
questions.tip: For a "why" detail question, find the cause sentence and match its paraphrase, ignoring choices that reverse it.
questions.trap: Choosing the reversed order (writing before reading) because the sentence mentions both skills.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that signature rates in marriage registers would be most useful for determining
choices: the exact share of a village that could read in a particular year
whether literacy in a region rose or fell over several decades
whether women read better than men in each parish
how many households owned prayer books
the age at which children began to learn to read
questions.explanation:
The inference follows from the two sentences about trends and "any given moment" in paragraph 3.

(A) Wrong: This is what paragraph 3 says the rates cannot do: they cannot establish how many could read "at any given moment".

**(B) Correct.** Paragraph 3: signature rates "remain a reliable guide to trends over time, since the gap between reading and writing probably changed slowly".

(C) Wrong: Unsupported. Women are mentioned only as a group likely to be undercounted.

(D) Wrong: Prayer books appear only in an illustrative example; ownership is not discussed.

(E) Wrong: The registers record signatures at marriage, not the start of reading instruction.
questions.tip: Distinguish what a measure can show (change over time) from what it cannot (absolute level).
questions.trap: Choosing the absolute-level answer, which is exactly what the historians say the method cannot provide.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of the passage ("Treating a signature count as a literacy rate, in short, mistakes a lower bound for a measurement") serves primarily to
choices: reject the use of marriage registers as historical evidence altogether
introduce an alternative proxy for estimating literacy
criticise the nineteenth-century scholars who first used the method
summarise the limitation of the method while implying that signature counts retain some value as a minimum estimate
argue that reading and writing were equally widespread
questions.explanation:
The sentence begins "in short", so it condenses the argument of paragraph 2 and the qualification in paragraph 3.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The author says the method has "real virtues" and remains reliable for trends.

(B) Wrong: No alternative proxy is offered anywhere in the passage.

(C) Wrong: The sentence criticises a misuse (treating counts as rates), not the scholars personally, and the passage does not single out the first users.

**(D) Correct.** "Lower bound" means signature counts show at least this many people were literate; that keeps their value as a floor while denying they are a full measurement.

(E) Wrong: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says reading was usually taught first and more widely.
questions.tip: On a final-sentence function question, summarise the whole paragraph and check which answer matches in both direction and strength.
questions.trap: Taking "mistakes" to mean wholesale rejection, when "lower bound" actually grants the method partial validity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
choices: Film composers have generally surpassed the opera composers whose idiom they inherited
A common criticism of film music is misplaced, because the film composer's distinctive achievement lies in solving problems peculiar to the medium
Max Steiner's scores are the finest examples of the Hollywood golden age
Most film scores are masterpieces despite constraints on the composer
Editors, rather than composers, determine the character of a film score
questions.explanation:
Map: P1 critics' charge of unoriginality; P2 author concedes the facts but reframes the difficulty; P3 qualifies and recommends a better question.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The author never ranks film composers above opera composers.

**(B) Correct.** This matches the "accurate as far as it goes" turn in paragraph 2 and the closing recommendation in paragraph 3.

(C) Wrong: Too narrow; Steiner is mentioned once, as an example of acknowledged debt.

(D) Wrong: Contradicted by paragraph 3: "None of this makes every film score a masterpiece."

(E) Wrong: Distortion. Editors fix scene lengths, which constrains the composer; the passage does not say they determine the music.
questions.tip: When an author concedes a point and then pivots ("accurate as far as it goes, but"), the main idea lives after the pivot.
questions.trap: Choosing the over-enthusiastic option; the author is a measured defender, not a cheerleader.

questions.prompt: Which of the following arguments is most similar in structure to the author's argument about film music?
choices: A critic argues that a novel is better than its film adaptation because the novel was written first
A coach insists that a team must copy its rivals' tactics exactly to compete
A chef admits that her recipes are traditional and claims they should therefore be praised
A reviewer argues that a stage play adapted for radio should be judged by how well it conveys action through sound alone, not by how much its plot differs from the original
A historian argues that all reproductions of old documents are unreliable
questions.explanation:
Principle: do not judge a work in one medium by the standards of another; ask how well it solves its own medium's problems (the sonnet-versus-novel line in paragraph 3).

(A) Wrong: This applies the same kind of standard the author criticises (priority and originality) rather than judging by the medium's demands.

(B) Wrong: Concerns imitation, not the choice of the right standard of judgment.

(C) Wrong: Praises tradition itself; the author says inheritance is acknowledged but beside the point.

**(D) Correct.** The author rejects an inappropriate standard (originality) and says the work should be judged by how well it solves the problems of its own medium. The reviewer does the same for radio.

(E) Wrong: Unrelated to judging a work by the standards of its own form.
questions.tip: Reduce the passage to an abstract pattern, then find the choice with the same pattern, not the same topic.
questions.trap: Choosing the film-versus-novel option because it shares the topic of adaptation while reversing the logic.

questions.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that the author regards the critics described in the first paragraph as
choices: mistaken about the extent of Wagner's influence on Hollywood composers
unaware that film scores must fit around dialogue and editing
right that most film music is formulaic and unoriginal
guilty of undervaluing opera composers
correct about the facts of borrowing but mistaken about what those facts show about the composer's achievement
questions.explanation:
The answer needs both halves: concession on facts, rejection of the inference drawn.

(A) Wrong: The author calls the charge "accurate as far as it goes", so the factual claim is accepted.

(B) Wrong: The passage does not say what the critics know, only that their charge overlooks the real difficulty.

(C) Wrong: The author concedes only that "the genre has produced its share of formulaic work", not "most".

(D) Wrong: Nothing in the passage suggests the critics undervalue opera.

**(E) Correct.** "Accurate as far as it goes" grants the factual claim; "mistakes the source of the film composer's difficulty" rejects the conclusion drawn from it.
questions.tip: When an author "partly agrees", separate what is conceded (facts) from what is denied (the conclusion).
questions.trap: Selecting an answer that makes the critics wrong about everything, ignoring the explicit concession.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that wolf reintroduction programmes should be abandoned
prove that grizzly bears, rather than wolves, caused the recovery of willows
describe how the number of elk in Yellowstone has changed since 1995
explain why conservation agencies favour reintroducing predators
show that a popular account of the ecological effects of wolf reintroduction is more contested than commonly assumed, and to indicate how such claims should be stated
questions.explanation:
The final sentence of the passage states the practical lesson: describe consequences "with the caution that the evidence, so far, allows".

(A) Wrong: Paragraph 3 says explicitly: "This is not an argument against reintroduction".

(B) Wrong: Too strong. Bears are one of several coinciding factors, and the passage proves nothing about a single cause.

(C) Wrong: Too narrow. Elk numbers are one detail in paragraph 2.

(D) Wrong: Misdirected. Agencies are mentioned in paragraph 3 only to show why the dispute has practical stakes.

**(E) Correct.** P1 gives the popular account, P2 the complications and the dispute, P3 the stakes and the closing call for caution.
questions.tip: Passages that move from "popular account" to "less tidy" usually have a purpose that combines the challenge and the recommended attitude.
questions.trap: Choosing an answer that turns the author's caution into a flat rejection of reintroduction.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the decline in elk numbers in Yellowstone
choices: began before the wolves had reached full strength and coincided with other developments
was caused mainly by hunting inside the park
was followed by an even recovery of willows along every stream
was predicted by no ecologist before 1995
began only after grizzly bears were removed from the park
questions.explanation:
Direct paraphrase of the first half of paragraph 2.

**(A) Correct.** Paragraph 2: "the decline began before the wolves arrived at full strength, and it coincided with a run of dry years, with hunting of elk outside the park, and with a recovery in the numbers of grizzly bears".

(B) Wrong: The hunting mentioned took place outside the park, and no main cause is identified.

(C) Wrong: Contradicts paragraph 2: the willow recovery has been "uneven".

(D) Wrong: The passage says ecologists did predict that wolves would reduce elk numbers.

(E) Wrong: Reversed. Grizzly bear numbers recovered over the period.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence containing the keyword; the right answer often lies in a list of factors.
questions.trap: Picking an option that borrows a word from the list (hunting) but moves it to the wrong place.

questions.prompt: The sceptics' reply described in the second paragraph implies that the association between taller willows and terrain with poor escape routes
choices: demonstrates that wolves have no effect on elk behaviour
might be explained by something other than the behaviour of wolves
proves that soil moisture is the sole cause of willow recovery
has been confirmed by experiments that controlled for soil moisture
shows that elk numbers did not decline after 1995
questions.explanation:
The reply offers an alternative explanation for the same pattern, so it weakens the inference to wolves without disproving it.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The sceptics offer an alternative possibility; they do not show that wolves have no effect.

**(B) Correct.** Sceptics say the pattern "would also arise if the willows were simply growing where the soil is wettest", an explanation that does not involve wolves.

(C) Wrong: Extreme. The reply says only that the pattern "would also arise" with wet soil.

(D) Wrong: No experiments are mentioned.

(E) Wrong: The passage grants that elk numbers did decline.
questions.tip: A reply of the form "this would also happen if..." introduces an alternative explanation, nothing more.
questions.trap: Overreading a rival hypothesis as a refutation.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that conservation agencies have drawn on the Yellowstone story primarily in order to
choices: criticise the agencies for knowingly misusing ecological data
show why the disagreement among researchers has practical consequences
offer evidence that wolves were the principal engine of recovery
suggest that agencies should halt reintroduction programmes
introduce the possibility that other predators affected the willows
questions.explanation:
Context: the sentence immediately before it is "The dispute is not merely academic."

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The author does not accuse agencies of misuse or of acting knowingly.

**(B) Correct.** The sentence follows "The dispute is not merely academic" and shows how agencies use the story to argue for reintroduction elsewhere.

(C) Wrong: The agencies' use of the story is not evidence about the cause; it is an example of the story's influence.

(D) Wrong: Contradicted by "This is not an argument against reintroduction".

(E) Wrong: Other predators are raised separately in the later "On the other hand" clause, not through the agencies.
questions.tip: For function questions, check the sentence that precedes the detail; it usually names the claim the detail supports.
questions.trap: Reading a neutral fact about agencies as an accusation.

questions.prompt: The author mentions the platform that hid each review until both parties had submitted primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the usual remedy of requesting more detailed ratings
demonstrate that temperament plays no role in ratings
provide evidence in support of the second diagnosis of ratings inflation
show that sellers are more honest than buyers by nature
argue that written criticism is more valuable than numerical ratings
questions.explanation:
The opening clause of the paragraph states the role of the example.

(A) Wrong: The platform changed the timing of reviews; it did not add rating detail.

(B) Wrong: Too strong. Paragraph 4 says "None of this proves that temperament plays no role".

**(C) Correct.** Paragraph 3 begins "Evidence for the second diagnosis comes from a platform..."

(D) Wrong: The passage attributes the sellers' candour to buyers having "little to fear", not to nature.

(E) Wrong: No such comparison is made; written criticism is mentioned only as an outcome that increased.
questions.tip: When a paragraph opens with "Evidence for X comes from...", the example's function is evidence for X.
questions.trap: Picking the over-strong conclusion (temperament plays no role) that the author explicitly refuses to draw.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a buyer with a modest complaint may leave a high rating because
choices: the seller could respond by giving the buyer a poor rating
buyers are generous by temperament
platforms require every buyer to give the maximum rating
detailed rating forms are too long to complete
sellers pay buyers for favourable reviews
questions.explanation:
Paraphrase of the second and third sentences of paragraph 2.

**(A) Correct.** Paragraph 2: a poor rating lets the seller "respond in kind", and the buyer "anticipates this".

(B) Wrong: This is the first (usual) diagnosis; the question concerns the structural reason in the second.

(C) Wrong: Invented; no such requirement is mentioned.

(D) Wrong: Form length is not discussed. The author says detail will not help because retaliation fear applies to every field.

(E) Wrong: Not mentioned anywhere.
questions.tip: Identify which diagnosis a detail question is asking about before choosing.
questions.trap: Choosing the first diagnosis (temperament) because it is stated first and sounds natural.

questions.prompt: A freelance platform, on which clients and freelancers rate one another, finds that nearly all ratings are five stars. Which of the following changes would the author most likely regard as promising?
choices: Adding five more categories to the rating form
Sending clients a reminder to be honest
Requiring clients to write at least 200 words with each rating
Providing a guide to how the five-star scale should be interpreted
Releasing each rating to the person rated only as part of a batch with many others, so that a reviewer cannot be easily identified and answered
questions.explanation:
Principle from paragraph 4: reforms should "remove the threat of retaliation, not merely ask reviewers to try harder".

(A) Wrong: The author says more detailed ratings "will do little" because fear of retaliation applies to every field.

(B) Wrong: The author criticises reforms that "merely ask reviewers to try harder".

(C) Wrong: Does not remove the threat of retaliation; it only asks more of the reviewer.

(D) Wrong: Another form of asking reviewers to try harder; it leaves the retaliation incentive untouched.

**(E) Correct.** The author favours reforms that "remove the threat of retaliation". Batching ratings makes retaliation much harder.
questions.tip: In application questions, derive the author's criterion for a good solution and test each option against it.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that asks more of reviewers, the approach the author has just dismissed.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely say that the result of the platform's rule change is consistent with the view that
choices: every inflated rating on every marketplace is caused by fear of retaliation
sellers are more honest than buyers by temperament
detailed ratings forms raise the average rating
buyers' reluctance to criticise sellers is at least partly a response to the platform's rules rather than a fixed trait
most buyers would give lower ratings if sellers' reviews were visible earlier
questions.explanation:
The experiment changed a rule, not reviewer character, and behaviour changed.

(A) Wrong: Extreme. Paragraph 4 says buyers differ and some will always be generous.

(B) Wrong: The passage explains sellers' candour as "presumably because buyers have little to fear", not as temperament.

(C) Wrong: Nothing in the passage suggests that detail raises ratings; the claim is that detail does little.

**(D) Correct.** Ratings fell and criticism doubled once the rules removed the retaliation threat, so the behaviour responds to incentives (paragraphs 3 and 4).

(E) Wrong: Reversed. The rule change hid the reviews until both were submitted.
questions.tip: If behaviour changes when incentives change, an inference about "fixed traits" is probably the answer being tested; use the author's hedges to avoid absolutes.
questions.trap: Choosing the "sellers are more honest" option, which sounds like a natural reading of the data but is contradicted by the author's own explanation.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that the standard account of the Green Revolution overstates the role of improved seed and neglects other conditions that shaped its outcomes
prove that guaranteed prices, rather than seed, were the decisive factor
describe how semi-dwarf varieties of wheat and rice were developed
show that the Green Revolution failed to raise grain output
compare the agricultural policies of Punjab with those of eastern India
questions.explanation:
Map: P1 standard story; P2 irrigation limits it; P3 policy matters too; P4 "necessary but not sufficient" and uneven benefits.

**(A) Correct.** P1 gives the standard narrative, P2 and P3 add irrigation and policy, P4 concludes that the seed was necessary but not sufficient.

(B) Wrong: The author says that claim "is hard to test" and probably cannot be settled.

(C) Wrong: Too narrow. The varieties are mentioned only as the starting point of the standard story.

(D) Wrong: Contradicts paragraph 1 and the tone of the passage, which accepts that the narrative "is not false".

(E) Wrong: Too narrow. The two regions are used in one paragraph to illustrate the role of irrigation, and policy is discussed nationally.
questions.tip: The main idea of a "revise the standard story" passage is that story is incomplete, not that it is false.
questions.trap: Choosing the bold single-cause claim; the author declines to crown any single factor.

questions.prompt: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the author's view of the role of improved seed in the Green Revolution?
choices: A vaccine that works equally well in every population regardless of health infrastructure
A new high-performance engine that improves a car's speed only when the car also has suitable tyres and fuel, so that the cars that gain most are those that have all three
A medicine whose success is attributed entirely to the government subsidy that made it affordable
A software package that is adopted widely because it is the cheapest on the market
A bridge that cuts travel time for all drivers by the same amount
questions.explanation:
Principle: a new element works only with complementary conditions; benefits accrue to those with the whole package.

(A) Wrong: The author's point is dependence on complementary conditions; this has none.

**(B) Correct.** The engine is necessary but not sufficient and its benefits go to those who can assemble the whole package, matching paragraph 4.

(C) Wrong: This resembles the economists' claim that prices alone were decisive, which the author considers hard to establish.

(D) Wrong: Explains adoption by a single feature, not by a package of conditions.

(E) Wrong: Benefits are uniform, unlike the uneven benefits in the passage.
questions.tip: Write the author's principle in abstract terms ("necessary but not sufficient, benefits follow the package") and test each analogy for both parts.
questions.trap: Choosing the single-cause option that mirrors the view the author treats with scepticism.

questions.prompt: The author refers to Punjab and eastern India primarily in order to
choices: show that the seeds performed poorly in every region
support the claim that guaranteed prices were the decisive element
contrast traditional seed with semi-dwarf varieties
illustrate how adoption of the new seed depended on irrigation that was already in place
argue that eastern India should have been given more fertiliser subsidies
questions.explanation:
The sentence that follows ("In this sense the geography of the Green Revolution was largely a geography of irrigation") states the point.

(A) Wrong: Contradicted by rapid adoption in Punjab.

(B) Wrong: Prices are discussed in paragraph 3 and not linked to the two regions.

(C) Wrong: The contrast in the passage is between regions with and without irrigation, using the same new seed.

**(D) Correct.** "Where canal or tube-well irrigation was already established, as in Punjab, adoption was rapid. Where it was not, as in much of eastern India..." The regions are examples of that claim.

(E) Wrong: No such recommendation appears in the passage.
questions.tip: Look at the sentence after an example for the author's own summary of what it shows.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that fits the topic but not the specific claim the regions were used to support.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following was part of the government arrangement that supported farmers' investment in costly inputs?
choices: A ban on grain imports
Free distribution of semi-dwarf seed to all farmers
Cancellation of debts owed by small farmers
Cheap electricity for pumping water
Restrictions on the use of canal water
questions.explanation:
A direct match to a sentence in paragraph 3.

(A) Wrong: Imports are mentioned only as the dependence that the revolution allowed India to leave behind.

(B) Wrong: Not mentioned. The seed is described as adopted by farmers, not given free.

(C) Wrong: Not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

**(D) Correct.** Paragraph 3: "Subsidised fertiliser and cheap electricity for pumping completed the arrangement."

(E) Wrong: Canals are mentioned as irrigation that predated the revolution, not as restricted.
questions.tip: For a list-style detail question, scan the paragraph that discusses the topic and match one item exactly.
questions.trap: Choosing a plausible policy that the passage never mentions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: The decline in brain volume is explained by the decline in body size
Several explanations have been offered for an apparent decline in human brain volume, each with limitations, and none should be treated as settled
Modern humans are less intelligent than their Ice Age ancestors
The apparent decline in brain volume is entirely a sampling artifact
Anthropologists have long troubled over how skulls should be measured
questions.explanation:
The final paragraph states the author's stance: "a mistake to treat any of these accounts as settled".

(A) Wrong: The author says the first explanation "falls short on its own terms".

**(B) Correct.** P1 states the puzzle; P2 to P4 describe and assess three explanations; P5 warns against treating any as settled.

(C) Wrong: The author warns against reading the decline "as evidence that modern humans think less well".

(D) Wrong: Proponents themselves concede the decline "would not vanish entirely", and the author treats no account as settled.

(E) Wrong: Distortion. What troubles anthropologists is the apparent decline, not the measurement method.
questions.tip: When a passage surveys several theories and ends with caution, the main idea is the survey plus the caution.
questions.trap: Choosing one of the three theories as "the" answer because it appears in the passage.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the second explanation described in the passage?
choices: Brain volume fell earlier and faster in regions where groups became larger and more specialised than in regions where groups stayed small
The skulls that have survived come mostly from unusually large individuals
Average body weight fell at the same time as brain volume
The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy in humans
Modern humans perform as well as Ice Age humans on tests of problem solving
questions.explanation:
The passage complains that the second explanation "makes few predictions that differ from those of its rivals", so the strongest support is a result that distinguishes it.

**(A) Correct.** The second explanation links smaller brains to growing, interdependent societies. A pattern in which the decline tracks social complexity supports that link and distinguishes it from the rival accounts.

(B) Wrong: This supports the third (statistical) explanation.

(C) Wrong: This is consistent with the first explanation and does not favour the social account over it.

(D) Wrong: Already stated in the passage as part of the argument; adding it does not strengthen it further.

(E) Wrong: Concerns capability, not what caused the decline, so it does not favour any explanation.
questions.tip: To strengthen a hypothesis, choose evidence that fits it and does not fit equally well with the rivals.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that fits several explanations equally; the passage itself shows this is why the second one is hard to test.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the first explanation falls short of explaining the decline in brain volume because
choices: the brain shrank by more than the usual relationship between brain size and body size would predict
people of the late Ice Age were lighter than their descendants
skulls from the late Ice Age are too rare to measure
brains consume too small a share of the body's energy
it makes the same predictions as its rivals
questions.explanation:
A direct match to a sentence in paragraph 2.

**(A) Correct.** Paragraph 2: "the brain shrank by more than the standard scaling between brain and body size would predict."

(B) Wrong: Reversed. The explanation assumes Ice Age people were more heavily built.

(C) Wrong: This is the basis of the third explanation, not a criticism of the first.

(D) Wrong: The energy figure belongs to the second explanation and is not a criticism of the first.

(E) Wrong: This is the criticism made of the second explanation.
questions.tip: On a "falls short because" question, match the author's stated criticism and watch for criticisms of other theories being swapped in.
questions.trap: Attaching the criticism of one explanation to another.

questions.prompt: The final paragraph of the passage implies which of the following?
choices: The organisation of the brain has been shown to matter more than its size
The skull data have been shown to be unreliable
A smaller brain volume does not by itself show lower cognitive ability
All three explanations are equally likely to be correct
Modern humans think as well as Ice Age humans did
questions.explanation:
The inference stays within the author's hedges ("crude proxy", "may matter more").

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The author says organisation "may matter more", not that this has been shown.

(B) Wrong: The author questions what the data can show, not whether it is unreliable.

**(C) Correct.** Brain volume is "a crude proxy", and the author warns against reading the decline as evidence that "modern humans think less well".

(D) Wrong: The author says none is settled but does not rank them as equal.

(E) Wrong: The author withholds judgement about thinking; the passage says only that the skull data do not speak to it.
questions.tip: If the passage says only that a measure is "crude", the safe inference is that it does not settle the underlying question.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that replaces "may" with "has been shown".

questions.prompt: The author mentions that some chains have sold company-owned outlets to franchisees primarily in order to
choices: show that franchising is cheaper than company ownership for every chain
illustrate how a salaried manager may lack incentive to work hard
argue that shortage of capital never plays a role in franchising decisions
suggest that hotel chains should franchise more outlets
provide evidence against a prediction made by the financial account of franchising
questions.explanation:
The sentence supports "The prediction has not held up well" at the start of paragraph 2.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The author lists costs of franchising in paragraph 3.

(B) Wrong: That illustration comes from the example of the slow Tuesday afternoon, not from the sales of outlets.

(C) Wrong: Contradicted by the last paragraph, which says shortage of capital may explain why chains start franchising.

(D) Wrong: Hotels are used to illustrate a limit of franchising, and no recommendation is made.

**(E) Correct.** The financial account predicts that chains with cheap capital will buy outlets back; the sales to franchisees show the opposite ("The prediction has not held up well").
questions.tip: Find which claim the detail serves: here, the sentence sits inside the case against the financial account.
questions.trap: Choosing the option that uses the right topic (incentives) from a different sentence.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following chains would be most likely to franchise its outlets?
choices: A chain of luxury hotels whose guests expect a consistent experience in every city
A chain of coffee shops whose outlets are all in the city where its headquarters stands
A chain of juice bars whose outlets are all in distant small towns and whose product does not depend on a tightly uniform customer experience
A chain of cinemas located next to its head office, run by salaried managers who are easily supervised
A chain whose brand would suffer sharply if any single outlet cut corners, and whose outlets are in the same district as its head office
questions.explanation:
Combine two conditions from the passage: monitoring is hard (remote) and the brand-damage cost is low.

(A) Wrong: Paragraph 3: hotels "often hold on to ownership even in distant locations".

(B) Wrong: Outlets near headquarters are easy to observe; the passage says such outlets tend to stay company-owned.

**(C) Correct.** Remote outlets are hard to monitor, which makes franchisee incentives valuable (paragraph 2 and 3), and low dependence on uniformity limits the brand-damage cost of franchising.

(D) Wrong: Near headquarters and easily supervised, so the incentive benefit of franchising is small.

(E) Wrong: Both factors point toward company ownership.
questions.tip: On inference questions with scenarios, list the two or three conditions the passage gives, then check each option against all of them.
questions.trap: Satisfying one condition (remoteness) while ignoring the other (need for uniform experience).

questions.prompt: Which of the following situations is most similar to the logic of the incentive account of franchising?
choices: A software firm pays its overseas sales agents mainly by commission, because it cannot easily observe how hard they work
A company borrows from a bank because it lacks the money to build a new factory
A manager receives a pay rise after an annual performance review
A bakery owner works long hours herself because she cannot afford to hire staff
A firm sells a division in order to repay its debts
questions.explanation:
Principle: when effort cannot be observed, pay for results by sharing the profit with the person who produces them.

**(A) Correct.** Effort that cannot be monitored is purchased by letting the agent keep part of the reward, which is the logic of the franchisee keeping the outlet's profit.

(B) Wrong: This is the financial account (shortage of capital), not the incentive account.

(C) Wrong: A review is a form of monitoring; the incentive account concerns situations where monitoring is hard.

(D) Wrong: This is a capital constraint, not a monitoring problem.

(E) Wrong: A financial motive, not an incentive motive.
questions.tip: Match the underlying mechanism (unobservable effort, shared reward), not the surface features (money, selling).
questions.trap: Choosing an option involving money and organisation without checking which account it matches.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a franchisee may be tempted to cut corners on quality because
choices: a franchisee is paid a fixed salary regardless of results
the head office cannot lend to franchisees at low interest rates
franchisees are always located far from headquarters
franchise contracts forbid any form of inspection
part of the damage to the brand falls on other outlets rather than on the franchisee
questions.explanation:
A direct match with the second sentence of paragraph 3.

(A) Wrong: This describes the salaried manager, not the franchisee, who keeps the profit.

(B) Wrong: Interest rates are not connected to quality in the passage.

(C) Wrong: Franchised outlets tend to be remote, but that is not the stated reason for cutting corners.

(D) Wrong: The passage says chains spend heavily on inspection and contracts to prevent corner-cutting.

**(E) Correct.** Paragraph 3: "the damage to the brand falls partly on other outlets".
questions.tip: Pick the reason the passage gives, not another true statement from the same paragraph.
questions.trap: Selecting remoteness, which is true of franchised outlets but is not the cause given for corner-cutting.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that cleaned paintings look closer to the artist's intention than uncleaned ones
describe the chemical process by which varnish darkens
evaluate opposing views about the cleaning of old paintings and propose a criterion that shifts the focus of the debate
condemn restorers for arrogance in claiming to know the artist's wishes
show that records of artists' intentions are usually reliable
questions.explanation:
The author criticises the framing of the debate ("This is mistaken") and then offers a new criterion in paragraph 4.

(A) Wrong: That is the restorers' position, which the author does not endorse.

(B) Wrong: Too narrow; varnish darkening is background in paragraph 1.

**(C) Correct.** P1 background; P2 critics; P3 restorers' reply and the author's objection to both; P4 the proposed criterion of reversibility.

(D) Wrong: The arrogance charge is attributed to critics, and the author criticises both sides.

(E) Wrong: Opposite; the author says intentions are "rarely documented".
questions.tip: When the author says "both sides tend to...", the main idea is about reframing, not choosing a side.
questions.trap: Choosing one side's position because it is described at length.

questions.prompt: The author states that the artist's intention "is rarely documented" primarily in order to
choices: show that the work of restorers is generally unreliable
cast doubt on the idea that intention alone can settle how a painting should be restored
prove that varnish should never be removed
explain why artists applied thin layers of glaze
urge historians to search for more documents about artists' wishes
questions.explanation:
The author is attacking the shared assumption of both sides that a single correct answer exists, so the sentence questions an assumption underlying both.

(A) Wrong: Too broad; the sentence concerns the intention criterion, not restorers' reliability.

**(B) Correct.** The sentence begins "Nor is it clear that the artist's intention... should be the only criterion", and the documentation point supports it.

(C) Wrong: The author does not argue against all cleaning, only against irreversible cleaning.

(D) Wrong: Glazes are discussed in paragraph 2 and the explanation is not related to documentation.

(E) Wrong: No such recommendation is made.
questions.tip: A "Nor is it clear that..." sentence is an author's qualification, so ask which assumption it questions.
questions.trap: Over-generalising the doubt into a rejection of restoration.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely regard a cleaning that restored a painting's original colours but permanently removed original glaze as
choices: a success, because it recovered the colour relationships the artist designed
open to serious objection on the author's own criterion, whatever its visual success
acceptable, provided that the removal was carefully recorded
objectionable only if the artist is known to have intended the glaze
irrelevant to the debate, since paintings change over time anyway
questions.explanation:
Apply the final paragraph's criterion (reversibility plus record) to a new case.

(A) Wrong: This is the restorers' viewpoint; the author judges by reversibility, not visual outcome alone.

**(B) Correct.** Paragraph 4: "Cleaning that destroys original material forecloses that freedom", and the "real failure" lies "in the irreversibility".

(C) Wrong: The author asks for interventions that are reversible and recorded; recording does not make destruction of original material acceptable.

(D) Wrong: The author says intention should not be the only criterion and rarely can be known.

(E) Wrong: The author says a painting's history is part of what it is, but still treats irreversible loss as a real failure.
questions.tip: When the question asks you to apply the author's criterion, read each option for both parts of the criterion, not just one.
questions.trap: Choosing the "recorded, so fine" option, which meets half of the criterion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following actions best reflects the approach recommended in the final paragraph?
choices: A museum scrapes away all later additions so that only the original paint remains, discarding what is removed
A museum leaves a darkened painting untouched out of respect for its history
A museum asks visitors to vote on how bright a restored painting should look
A museum fills gaps in a damaged painting with removable paint and documents exactly what was added
A museum permanently repaints missing sections to match the surrounding colours
questions.explanation:
Final paragraph: "Interventions that are reversible, and carefully recorded, leave later generations free to judge differently."

(A) Wrong: This destroys material irreversibly and leaves no record of what was lost.

(B) Wrong: The author does not argue for avoiding all intervention, only for reversible and recorded interventions.

(C) Wrong: The author moves away from debating the appearance toward whether interventions can be undone.

**(D) Correct.** It is reversible and recorded, so later generations are free to judge differently.

(E) Wrong: Permanent repainting cannot be undone.
questions.tip: Translate the recommendation into a checklist (reversible, recorded) and test each option.
questions.trap: Choosing the option that sounds respectful but is not what the author recommends.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that artificial light is harmless to wildlife
explain why moths are attracted to lamps
report a study of how artificial light affects plant pollination and note the limits of its findings
show that bees and hoverflies are better pollinators than moths
demonstrate that plants with long, narrow flowers cannot be pollinated at night
questions.explanation:
Map: P1 prediction; P2 study results (moth visits down, seeds down only a little); P3 caveat about specialised plants.

(A) Wrong: Contradicted by paragraph 3: "The authors do not conclude that artificial light is harmless."

(B) Wrong: Outside scope. The attraction is mentioned only as background.

**(C) Correct.** P1 sets up the prediction; P2 reports the study; P3 gives the authors' caveats.

(D) Wrong: The passage says only that daytime pollinators made up much of the difference, not that they are better.

(E) Wrong: Distortion. The authors suggest such plants may be more vulnerable; the study did not test them.
questions.tip: In a "study, then caveat" passage, the purpose answer pairs the report with the limitation.
questions.trap: Picking the "harmless" answer because the seed figures look small.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in the lit plots
choices: moth visits and seed production both fell by about three-fifths
seed production rose because daytime pollinators visited more often
moth visits to flowers fell by about three-fifths, while seed production fell by about one-eighth
visits by hoverflies and bees fell along with visits by moths
moth visits fell by about one-eighth while seed production fell by about three-fifths
questions.explanation:
A direct match with two sentences in paragraph 2.

(A) Wrong: Seed production fell far less.

(B) Wrong: Seed production fell; daytime visits only made up much of the difference.

**(C) Correct.** Paragraph 2: "Visits by moths in the lit plots fell by about three-fifths. Yet the number of seeds... fell by only about one-eighth."

(D) Wrong: The passage says daytime pollinators visited in greater numbers.

(E) Wrong: The two figures are swapped.
questions.tip: When a question combines two numbers, check that each number is attached to the right quantity.
questions.trap: Swapped or merged figures.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the plants most vulnerable to harm from artificial light are those
choices: that flower only during the day
that produce the most seeds
