that depend on moths because few other species can reach their flowers
that grow in meadows in southern England
that are pollinated mainly by bees
questions.explanation:
The authors' caveat in paragraph 3 identifies where compensation by other pollinators would fail.

(A) Wrong: Daytime flowers are visited by daytime pollinators, which the lamps do not remove.

(B) Wrong: Seed quantity is not linked to vulnerability in the passage.

**(C) Correct.** Paragraph 3: plants with long, narrow flowers that "only a few species of moth can reach" may be affected much more, since other pollinators cannot compensate.

(D) Wrong: The study sites are not claimed to be more vulnerable; their plants were generally pollinated by many species.

(E) Wrong: Bees visited more when moths were absent, so these plants are unlikely to be the most vulnerable.
questions.tip: The group most at risk is the one for which the "compensation" explanation does not apply.
questions.trap: Choosing a group named in the passage but for which the effect is expected to be small.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that the slower growth in starting salaries was concentrated in firms that previously paid above the market primarily in order to
choices: show that the policy has failed to achieve its purpose
support the advocates' prediction about pay gaps
demonstrate that most firms in the study paid above the market
suggest a mechanism by which disclosure may lead to lower starting salaries
criticise firms for having relied on secrecy
questions.explanation:
Look at the clause that follows: "suggesting that disclosure leads such firms to stop outbidding".

(A) Wrong: The author says it would be "premature to read these results as a verdict".

(B) Wrong: The pay gap result is given separately; this detail supports the critics' side.

(C) Wrong: No claim is made about how many firms paid above the market.

**(D) Correct.** The following clause says disclosure may lead such firms "to stop outbidding their rivals", which offers a mechanism.

(E) Wrong: The passage describes behaviour and does not criticise it.
questions.tip: The clause after "suggesting that" usually states what the detail is meant to show.
questions.trap: Taking a finding for the critics as a verdict on the policy.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that disclosure would have the smallest effect on starting salaries in a market in which
choices: employers' pay was already widely known before disclosure was required
most firms had previously relied heavily on secret negotiation to attract workers
many firms had previously paid well above the market
the studies cover a very long period
workers hired at the top of a range outnumber those hired at the bottom
questions.explanation:
The conclusion that effects depend on prior reliance on secrecy gives the answer by contrast.

**(A) Correct.** The author says effects "depend on how much employers were previously able to rely on secrecy"; where pay was already known, there is little secrecy to lose.

(B) Wrong: This is the condition under which the effect should be larger.

(C) Wrong: The slower growth was concentrated in exactly such firms.

(D) Wrong: Study length affects what can be concluded, not the size of the effect in a market.

(E) Wrong: Distribution of hires is not tied to the size of the overall effect.
questions.tip: When the author says "depends on X", the smallest effect occurs when X is smallest.
questions.trap: Reversing the dependency and choosing the high-secrecy case.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most analogous to the behaviour of above-market firms after disclosure, as the author describes it?
choices: A restaurant lowers its prices after customers complain that they are too high
A university sees applications rise after publishing its graduates' salaries
A company hides its profits so that it pays less tax
A retailer that offered quiet, undisclosed discounts to win customers from rivals reduces them after a new rule makes all its discounts public, because rivals can now match them at once
A drug manufacturer cuts prices when its patent expires and generic makers enter the market
questions.explanation:
The mechanism: secret premium offers win people from rivals; visibility lets rivals respond, so the premium stops.

(A) Wrong: Responds to complaints, not to rivals seeing and matching its offers.

(B) Wrong: Disclosure here increases demand; it has nothing to do with rivals matching secret advantages.

(C) Wrong: Concealment for tax purposes; no rivals or outbidding.

**(D) Correct.** Secrecy had allowed the firm to outbid rivals quietly; once its offers are visible, rivals can match and the firm's incentive to outbid disappears.

(E) Wrong: Competition arrives through the patent expiry, not through the visibility of the firm's offers.
questions.tip: State the mechanism in steps (secret advantage, made visible, rivals respond, advantage disappears) and match each step.
questions.trap: Choosing a scenario that merely involves prices or disclosure without the "rivals can now match" step.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: prove that shorter antibiotic courses are safe for every infection
explain how tuberculosis is treated with antibiotics
criticise doctors for repeating a long-standing instruction
recommend that patients stop taking antibiotics as soon as symptoms fade
present a challenge to a traditional medical recommendation, report how its defenders respond, and reach a measured conclusion about what patients should do
questions.explanation:
The last sentence of the passage states the conclusion: follow your own doctor "rather than to adopt either slogan".

(A) Wrong: Contradicted by paragraph 3 and paragraph 4: the trials involved mild infections, and few researchers claim shortest-possible treatment for all.

(B) Wrong: Too narrow. Tuberculosis is mentioned only as the origin of the recommendation.

(C) Wrong: The author does not criticise doctors; the final advice is to follow one's own doctor.

(D) Wrong: The defenders' point is that stopping at symptom relief is different from a properly shortened course, and the author does not endorse it.

**(E) Correct.** P1 the advice; P2 the challenge (evidence and theory); P3 the defenders' reply; P4 the narrowed disagreement and the practical conclusion.
questions.tip: A passage that moves through claim, challenge, reply and compromise has a purpose that covers all four.
questions.trap: Picking a bold position that belongs to only one side.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, critics of the traditional advice argue that long courses of antibiotics may increase resistance because
choices: a few bacteria survive an early stop and then multiply
tuberculosis becomes harder to treat with longer courses
patients with weakened immune systems take longer courses
harmless gut bacteria are exposed to the drug for longer, which gives resistance more opportunity to develop
longer courses work less well than shorter ones in all patients
questions.explanation:
A paraphrase of the "second objection" in paragraph 2.

(A) Wrong: This is the traditional reasoning for finishing the course, not the critics' argument.

(B) Wrong: Tuberculosis is mentioned as the source of the original recommendation, not as evidence for the critics' resistance argument.

(C) Wrong: Not stated; weakened immune systems appear in the defenders' reply.

**(D) Correct.** Paragraph 2: "the longer the many harmless bacteria in the gut are exposed to it... that exposure... is where resistance is most likely to develop".

(E) Wrong: The trials found short courses worked "about as well" in "most" patients, not that long courses work worse.
questions.tip: Distinguish the critics' theory from the traditional theory; both are in the same paragraph.
questions.trap: Choosing the traditional reasoning because it appears first in the passage and is easy to recall.

questions.prompt: The defenders' observation that stopping treatment is not the same as being prescribed a shorter course serves primarily to
choices: prove that the traditional advice is correct for all infections
concede that shorter courses are generally less effective
argue that patients cannot be trusted to follow instructions
indicate that the new trials do not directly test what happens when patients stop treatment early
support the critics' claim about the origin of the recommendation
questions.explanation:
The sentence undercuts how far the trial evidence applies to the behaviour the traditional advice addresses.

(A) Wrong: Too strong. The point limits the relevance of the trials; it does not prove the traditional advice.

(B) Wrong: The passage says shorter courses were "about as well" in most trial patients.

(C) Wrong: No such claim is made.

**(D) Correct.** The trials gave short courses of the correct length from the start; patients who stop when symptoms fade are in a different position.

(E) Wrong: The origin of the recommendation (tuberculosis) is raised by critics and is not related to this observation.
questions.tip: A "not the same as" observation usually draws a boundary around what a piece of evidence shows.
questions.trap: Over-reading a limitation on evidence as a proof of the opposing claim.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most analogous to the critics' first objection (concerning evidence) to the traditional advice?
choices: A safety rule for all bridges that was derived from tests on one unusual type of bridge and was never tested on other types
A building code based on tests of many different types of building
A diet recommended widely because it has become fashionable
A medicine approved after trials covering many kinds of illness
A teaching method that worked in one school and was later confirmed in several others
questions.explanation:
Principle: a rule drawn from a special case was applied to other cases without direct testing.

**(A) Correct.** The recommendation arose from work on one unusual disease and was extended to others "with little direct testing".

(B) Wrong: The objection is about a narrow evidence base, and this code has a broad one.

(C) Wrong: The problem is popularity, not the extension of narrow evidence to other cases.

(D) Wrong: Broad testing does not match the narrow-evidence objection.

(E) Wrong: The method was re-tested; the critics' complaint is that the antibiotic advice was not.
questions.tip: The analogy must contain both the special origin and the untested extension.
questions.trap: Choosing a scenario about general weak evidence rather than the specific pattern of untested extension.

questions.prompt: Which of the following situations is most analogous to the change described in the second paragraph?
choices: A town where attendance at a public lecture series fell because residents lost interest in the topic
A town where community cookery classes have closed, but people still share recipes and learn techniques through small informal video groups
A town where the library closed and no other source of books is available to residents
A town where a club increased its membership after introducing a fee
A town where several small clubs merged into one large, formal association
questions.explanation:
Principle: falling membership in formal bodies does not prove falling connection, because the connection has taken informal forms.

(A) Wrong: The activity itself declined; there is no shift to a new form.

**(B) Correct.** The older institution declined, yet the underlying activity continues in a different, informal form, as with civic ties in paragraph 2.

(C) Wrong: The activity has genuinely ended, which is the gloomy reading the author questions.

(D) Wrong: No decline in the institution and no shift to informal forms.

(E) Wrong: The shift is toward a larger formal body, not toward informal connection.
questions.tip: Define the pattern as "institution declines, activity persists in another form" and filter the options.
questions.trap: Choosing an option with a decline but no persistence of the activity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
choices: Social connection has increased as formal associations declined, and this should be welcomed
Falling membership in civic associations does not by itself show weaker social connection, but the informal replacements raise questions about who is included
Formal associations were dull and exclusive, and their decline is no loss
Sociologists have exaggerated the decline in membership numbers
Informal networks are better than formal associations at including newcomers
questions.explanation:
Final paragraph: the useful question is "what kinds of connection are available to whom".

(A) Wrong: Too positive. Paragraph 3 begins "It would be too easy to conclude that nothing has been lost".

**(B) Correct.** It covers the challenge to the gloomy inference (P2) and the concern about inclusion (P3 and P4).

(C) Wrong: Paragraph 3 says the older institutions gave strangers "a reason to meet and a framework for resolving disputes".

(D) Wrong: Paragraph 1 grants that "the numbers are real".

(E) Wrong: Opposite. Informal networks "need admit no one" and "offer little protection" to outsiders.
questions.tip: A balanced author's main point usually has two parts joined by "but".
questions.trap: Choosing the cheerful half of the author's argument without the concern.

questions.prompt: The author mentions "a club that met on the first Monday of each month" primarily in order to
choices: show that clubs were more effective at building trust than any modern group
criticise club members for attending too rarely
argue that clubs should hold meetings more frequently
prove that membership numbers have fallen
illustrate the older, formal kind of association with which the newer informal groups are contrasted
questions.explanation:
The "Where... a present-day resident is more likely..." structure shows the example is one half of a contrast.

(A) Wrong: The comparison concerns form, and the author does not claim clubs built more trust.

(B) Wrong: The monthly meeting is a description, not a criticism.

(C) Wrong: No such recommendation is made.

(D) Wrong: The decline in numbers is stated in paragraph 1 and does not depend on this example.

**(E) Correct.** It is introduced with "Where an earlier generation joined a club..." and set against the neighbourhood messaging group.
questions.tip: An example introduced by "Where an earlier generation..." is almost always one side of an old-versus-new contrast.
questions.trap: Treating a descriptive detail as an evaluative one.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, informal networks tend to
choices: be governed by written constitutions
admit any newcomer who meets certain conditions
collect dues and keep minutes
have declined in membership over several decades
form among people who are already similar in age, income and outlook
questions.explanation:
A direct match with a sentence in paragraph 3.

(A) Wrong: Written constitutions belong to formal associations.

(B) Wrong: This describes formal associations; informal groups "need admit no one".

(C) Wrong: Paragraph 2 says informal groups have "no officers, no dues and no minutes".

(D) Wrong: The decline described concerns formal associations.

**(E) Correct.** Paragraph 3: "They tend to form among people who are already similar in age, income and outlook".
questions.tip: Make sure the feature is attributed to the right type of group; the passage contrasts two types.
questions.trap: Choosing a feature of the formal association.
